title: Elites Shouldn’t Bury Their Talents in the Ground
author: Aaron M. Renn
summary: Aaron Renn's digest centres on Edan Krolewicz's essay arguing that American elites have won conventionally yet done little with their abilities, and on Renn's own commentary that selection for conscientiousness and risk aversion forms elites to climb rather than question. He stresses the distinction between generic help (volunteering at a food bank) and deploying rare skills, which is riskier personally and politically. He then covers R. R. Reno's First Things piece on training elites, James Davison Hunter's Hedgehog Review call for a "third founding", which Renn finds strong on diagnosis and weak on solutions and likens to his own "American Transition", and a Foreign Affairs essay that treats children as a luxury good and expects fertility decline to deepen inequality between nations. He notes an IFS report tying celebrity culture to fertility decline in Japan and Korea, and teases a paywalled section on middle-class affordability.
points: Renn, following Krolewicz, argues that meritocratic selection itself forms elites into skilled climbers who do not question the game.
The moral claim is that those with extraordinary skills, resources and networks must defend burying them, rather than the other way around.
He contrasts generic volunteer help with using the specific, rare abilities that make a person distinctive.
Hunter's "third founding" and Renn's "American Transition" both express a sense that current institutions and culture no longer fit their purpose.
The Foreign Affairs piece frames children as a luxury good, so fertility decline could produce demographic inequality between countries.
quotes: Someone sent me this interesting piece from earlier this year by Edan Krolewicz arguing that American elites have betrayed their own potential.

The lawyer who questions the adversarial system doesn’t make partner. By the time someone reaches elite status, decades of selection have produced exactly the traits that make them good at climbing and useless at questioning. [emphasis added]
Some people are content to invest their talents in the bank and earn enough interest to prove they did their duty.
While religion no longer provides a common epistemic, metaphysical, or even ethical horizon, autonomous reason does no better.

An interesting essay in Foreign Affairs looks at the global implications of the fertility bust, arguing that it will result in increased inequality between nations. The author starts by noting that as children today are costly but produce no economic benefits, they are in effect a luxury good.

This is already happening in the Americas: among countries with at least 20 million inhabitants, the United States has the highest fertility rate in the hemisphere, well ahead of Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Colombia, and Mexico, and matched only by Peru, whose fertility rate is plummeting fast. (Venezuela’s official fertility rate is pure fiction.)
